mechanism_narrative: WORKPLACES mobility has risen roughly 8 points over the last four weeks (-33.4 to -25.4), indicating resumed commuting routines. This commute-driven foot traffic spills over into nearby retail and recreation visits, pushing RETAIL_REC higher over the next four weeks.
failure_condition: RETAIL_REC fails to rise, or falls, over the next 28 days despite WORKPLACES continuing its upward trend over the same period.

mechanism_narrative: TRANSIT usage recovering past a critical threshold (above -45% of baseline) indicates restored reliance on public transport, enabling more trips to retail and recreation destinations within two weeks.
candidate_trigger: TRANSIT weekly mean rises above -45 for two consecutive weeks
evidence_refs: fact: TRANSIT improved from -51.0 at t-3w to -43.6 at t-0w
failure_condition: RETAIL_REC does not increase in the two weeks following TRANSIT crossing -45, or declines despite the threshold being met.

mechanism_narrative: A simultaneous decline in RESIDENTIAL time-at-home and rise in WORKPLACES mobility together indicate a broader behavioral shift away from home-centric routines, compounding to increase discretionary retail and recreation visits more than either series would alone.
candidate_trigger: RESIDENTIAL declines while WORKPLACES rises concurrently for two consecutive weeks
failure_condition: RETAIL_REC does not rise even when RESIDENTIAL declines and WORKPLACES rises concurrently over consecutive weeks.

mechanism_narrative: The sharp spike in PARKS mobility (reaching 43.0 at t-2w) reflects seasonal or weather-driven outdoor recreation that substitutes for indoor retail and recreation visits, temporarily suppressing RETAIL_REC in the following week.
candidate_trigger: PARKS weekly mean rises more than 20 points above the prior week's mean
evidence_refs: fact: PARKS jumped from 15.9 at t-3w to 43.0 at t-2w
failure_condition: RETAIL_REC rises in the week following a PARKS spike greater than 20 points, rather than falling.

mechanism_narrative: A sustained improvement in GROCERY_PHARM mobility signals loosening of essential-business restrictions at the policy level, which typically precedes relaxation of restrictions on non-essential retail, raising RETAIL_REC within two weeks.
candidate_trigger: GROCERY_PHARM weekly mean improves by more than 5 points week-on-week in two consecutive weeks
evidence_refs: fact: GROCERY_PHARM rose from -22.6 at t-1w to -17.1 at t-0w
failure_condition: RETAIL_REC does not increase within two weeks after GROCERY_PHARM meets the improvement threshold twice consecutively.

mechanism_narrative: If TRANSIT and WORKPLACES both reverse their recent improvement and decline simultaneously, this signals a re-tightening of mobility restrictions, which would reduce RETAIL_REC over the following four weeks as people curtail non-essential trips.
candidate_trigger: TRANSIT and WORKPLACES both fall for two consecutive weeks
failure_condition: RETAIL_REC continues to rise despite simultaneous declines in TRANSIT and WORKPLACES for two consecutive weeks.

mechanism_narrative: RESIDENTIAL mobility has been declining steadily (14.9 to 9.4) indicating reduced home-confinement behavior; this always-on trend predicts continued increases in RETAIL_REC as people spend proportionally more time away from home.
evidence_refs: fact: RESIDENTIAL fell from 14.9 at t-3w to 9.4 at t-0w
failure_condition: RETAIL_REC fails to increase over the next 28 days despite continued decline in RESIDENTIAL.

mechanism_narrative: PARKS mobility shows high week-to-week variance driven by weather; when PARKS reverts toward its local trend after a large spike, previously suppressed retail demand rebounds, lifting RETAIL_REC within the following week.
candidate_trigger: PARKS weekly mean falls back toward its 4-week average after a spike exceeding 35
evidence_refs: fact: PARKS spiked to 43.0 at t-2w then fell to 17.3 at t-1w while RETAIL_REC fell from -33.1 to -35.7
failure_condition: RETAIL_REC does not rise in the week following a PARKS reversion from a spike exceeding 35 back toward baseline.
